section_1.title: The Hook: The Limits of Average
section_1.content: Introduce the problem of measuring speed. Explain that average speed (total distance / total time) fails to describe the instantaneous state of motion. Establish the prerequisite: Understanding linear slope (rate of change).
section_1.example: A cheetah chasing prey: 'Average speed' tells us how fast it ran over 10 seconds, but not how fast it was going at the exact moment it pounced.

section_2.title: The Derivative: Magnifying the Instant
section_2.content: Visualize the 'Zooming In' process. As the time interval shrinks toward zero, the secant line on a graph morphs into a tangent line. This is the birth of the derivative: measuring instantaneous change.
section_2.example: An animation showing a curve of the cheetah's position; as we zoom in on a single point, the curve looks like a straight line, representing the instantaneous velocity.

section_3.title: The Integral: Summing the Infinite
section_3.content: Introduce the area problem. Explain that while it's easy to calculate the area of rectangles, curved shapes are difficult. We approximate using many thin rectangles; as their width approaches zero, the sum becomes the 'Integral'.
section_3.example: Calculating the total distance traveled by a robot whose speed changes constantly by summing the tiny 'area' strips of speed × time under its velocity-time graph.

section_4.title: The Fundamental Theorem: The Bridge
section_4.content: Reveal the 'Secret Connection': Differentiation (breaking things down) and Integration (putting them together) are inverse processes, much like addition and subtraction.
section_4.example: Visualizing the robot's journey: Integrating the velocity curve gives us the total distance traveled, while differentiating the distance curve gives us back the velocity.

section_5.title: Conclusion: The Language of Change
section_5.content: Summarize that calculus is the mathematical study of continuous change. It allows us to predict the future of dynamic systems, from planetary orbits to AI optimization.
section_5.example: A final visual showing how calculus allows us to calculate not just where a rocket is, but exactly how much fuel it needs to land precisely on a moving platform.
